note: Continuous timeline: sequence numbers run 1-11 for FREN151 (weeks 1-11) then 11-23 for FREN152 (weeks 2-13, since FREN152's own week 1 has no separate tutorial content).

topics.title: Gender & articles (un/une/des, le/la/les/l')
topics.rule: Nouns are masculine or feminine. A: un (m) / une (f) / des (pl). THE: le (m) / la (f) / les (pl); both le and la become l' before a vowel or silent h.

items.en: How do you say ... in French?

items.fr: Vous pouvez réexpliquer, s'il vous plaît?
items.en: Can you explain that again please?
see you / see you next time

topics.title: Regular verb conjugation groups
topics.rule: French has three groups of regular verbs, named after their infinitive endings: -er, -ir, -re.

topics.title: -er verb conjugation (parler)
topics.rule: Remove -ER from the infinitive to get the stem, then add: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.

topics.title: Asking someone's nationality

items.en: I am an Australian of Lebanese extraction.

topics.rule: Feminine nationality usually adds -e (unless already ending in e); nationalities ending in -ien add -enne. Plural: add -s (masc./mixed) or -es (fem.); already-s endings don't double.

topics.title: Elision and liaison
topics.rule: Elision: a final vowel is dropped and replaced with an apostrophe before a word starting with a vowel or silent h (je, le, la, de, que, ne, se, ce, si). Liaison: a normally-silent final consonant is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel.

topics.title: Reflexive (pronominal) verbs
topics.rule: Reflexive verbs take a reflexive pronoun immediately before the verb, matching the subject.

topics.title: Uses of 'pour'

items.en: I am studying French to travel

topics.rule: 'Pour' translates 'for', or 'in order to' when followed by an infinitive.

items.fr: agent de police / agente de police

topics.title: Asking someone's occupation

items.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu fais dans la vie?
items.en: What do you do for a living? (informal)

items.fr: Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie?
items.en: What do you do for a living? (formal)

topics.rule: No article (un/une) before an occupation after 'être' or 'travailler comme' — e.g. 'Je suis professeur', not 'Je suis un professeur'. But an article IS used after 'c'est': 'C'est une actrice'.

items.fr: Je travaille à temps plein / complet.

topics.title: 'From' and 'to' with countries
topics.rule: Countries ending in -e are almost always feminine; others are masculine. de/d' (fem.), du (masc.), des (plural) = 'from'. en (fem.), au (masc.), aux (plural) = 'to/in'. Towns/cities use de and à regardless of gender.

topics.title: Aller (to go) and Venir (to come)
topics.rule: Aller and venir are irregular and must be memorised.

topics.title: Numbers 60-100
topics.rule: French counts 70-99 in base-20 style: soixante-dix (60+10), quatre-vingts (4x20), quatre-vingt-dix (4x20+10).

items.fr: Quel est ton/votre numéro de téléphone?

topics.title: The negative (ne...pas)

items.en: I don't have a tablet. (un/une/des → de after negative)
It isn't a smartphone. (être keeps un/une)

topics.rule: 'ne' and 'pas' surround the conjugated verb. After ne...pas, un/une/des become just 'de' — except with the verb être.

items.fr: Est-ce que tu as un ordinateur?
Pour aller à (au/à la/aux/à l')..., s'il vous plaît?
items.en: How do I get to..., please?

topics.title: Vivre (to live)
topics.rule: Habiter is used only for the place/building you live in. Vivre is broader: place, 'to be alive', 'to live through', manner of living.

topics.title: Places in a town II (water, worship, streets)
Giving an opinion on a city
il y a / il n'y a pas de

items.fr: Il n'y a pas de théâtre.

topics.rule: Il y a + un/une/des for affirmative; il n'y a pas de/d' for negative (article dropped).

topics.title: Prepositions of place

items.fr: à côté du / de la / de l' / des

topics.rule: Longer prepositions ending in 'de' combine with the definite article: de+le→du, de+les→des, de+la/l' stay the same.

topics.title: Expressions of quantity
topics.rule: After an expression of quantity, no article is used — just the plural noun (quelques églises, beaucoup de magasins). Exceptions: un hôpital→des hôpitaux, un centre commercial→des centres commerciaux keep irregular plurals.

topics.title: Position of adjectives (BAGS)
topics.rule: Most adjectives come AFTER the noun (un quartier dynamique). BAGS adjectives (Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size) come BEFORE the noun instead (une belle ville, un petit parc).

topics.title: Adverbs modifying adjectives
topics.rule: Adverbs like assez/très are placed before the adjective they modify: c'est un quartier assez agréable.

topics.title: Elision rule (recap)
topics.rule: Elision (je, me, te, se, le, la, ce, ne, de, que, si) drops the final vowel before a word starting with a vowel or silent h.

topics.title: Nationalities & capitalisation

items.en: I speak French and German. (lowercase language)
The Germans are hard-working. (capitalised noun for people)

topics.rule: Nationality adjectives and language names are lowercase in French; nouns referring to the people of a nation are capitalised.

topics.title: à/de + definite article contractions
topics.rule: à+la and à+l', de+la and de+l' do NOT contract — only le and les contract.

items.en: I am a student. (no article before occupation)
I like tennis. (definite article after like/dislike verbs)
I don't have a car. (un/une/des → de after negation)
It isn't a Hyundai. (être keeps un/une in the negative)

topics.title: Verb placement rules

items.en: I like to swim. (2nd verb stays infinitive)

items.fr: Je n'aime pas faire de l'équitation.
items.en: I don't like horse-riding. (ne...pas surrounds the FIRST verb)

topics.rule: With two verbs in a row, only the first is conjugated; the second stays in the infinitive. Negation wraps the first (conjugated) verb only.

topics.title: aussi (also/too) placement

items.fr: J'adore nager, j'aime aussi faire du surf.
items.en: I love swimming, I also like surfing.

topics.rule: 'Aussi' meaning 'also/too' goes AFTER the verb, never at the start of a sentence (starting with aussi changes its meaning to 'therefore').

items.en: The book is good. (bon/bonne describes a noun)

items.fr: le frère cadet / la sœur cadette
le frère aîné / la sœur aînée

topics.title: Possessive adjectives
topics.rule: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they precede, not the owner's gender. Mon/ton/son are also used before feminine words starting with a vowel sound (mon amie).

items.fr: Combien de personnes y a-t-il dans ta famille?
items.en: How many people are in your family?

items.fr: As-tu des frères ou des sœurs?
items.en: Do you have brothers or sisters?

topics.title: Possessive with 'de' (Elizabeth's boyfriend)
topics.rule: French has no 's; use [thing] + de + [owner]. 'De' contracts with le/les into du/des.

topics.title: Verbs of like/dislike + infinitive
topics.rule: Verbs of like/dislike are followed by an infinitive (j'aime nager) or, if a noun, the definite article (j'aime le tennis). préférer has an accent change (è vs é) but regular endings.

topics.title: Physical attributes
topics.rule: The definite article (les) is required before 'hair' and 'eyes' in French, unlike in English.

topics.title: Regular adjective agreement

items.fr: drôle (masc./fem. sg, ends in silent e)

topics.rule: Regular adjectives: masc. sg = base form; fem. sg = base+e; masc. pl = base+s; fem. pl = base+es. Adjectives already ending in silent -e don't add another e in the feminine.

topics.title: Il est / Elle est vs C'est

items.en: He's a teacher. (il est + occupation, no article)

items.fr: Mon frère, il est à Paris.
items.en: My brother is in Paris. (il/elle est + preposition for place)

topics.rule: C'est + noun; Il/Elle est + adjective, occupation (no article), or place preposition. Il/elle can also mean 'it' when referring back to an object.

topics.title: Telling the time

items.fr: Il est cinq heures moins vingt de l'après-midi.

topics.rule: French can express time two ways: 12hr clock with du matin/de l'après-midi/du soir, or the 24hr clock (more common in writing/timetables).

topics.title: Numbers 60 to a billion
topics.rule: 'Et' is only used in double-digit numbers ending in 1 (21, 31, 41, 51, 61, 71) — never in larger numbers like 301 (trois cent un) or 5023 (cinq mille vingt-trois).

topics.title: The present tense: -ir and -re verbs

items.fr: je finis / tu finis / il finit
items.en: I/you/he finish(es) (-ir pattern, e.g. finir, choisir, réussir, grossir, maigrir, réfléchir)

items.fr: nous finissons / vous finissez / ils finissent
je vends / tu vends / il vend
items.en: I/you/he sell(s) (-re pattern, e.g. vendre, attendre, répondre, rendre, perdre)

items.fr: nous vendons / vous vendez / ils vendent

topics.rule: -ir verbs (like finir): stem + is, is, it, issons, issez, issent. -re verbs (like vendre): stem + s, s, [nothing], ons, ez, ent.

topics.title: Days of the week
topics.rule: Days of the week are NOT capitalised in French, unlike English.

items.en: on Mondays (habitually) vs. lundi = on [one particular] Monday

items.fr: le matin / le midi / l'après-midi / le soir
items.en: in the mornings/at noon/in the afternoons/in the evenings (habitually)

topics.title: jouer à / jouer de / faire de

items.fr: jouer au rugby / au tennis / aux échecs
jouer du piano / de la guitare
faire du vélo / de la natation
items.en: to do cycling/swimming (general activities take 'faire de')

topics.rule: jouer à + le/la/les/l' → au/à la/aux/à l' for sports and games. jouer de + le/la/les/l' → du/de la/des/de l' for musical instruments.

topics.title: Adverbs and phrases of frequency
topics.rule: One-word adverbs (jamais, souvent, toujours, etc.) go after the verb (Je vais toujours en cours); in the negative, after 'pas' (Je ne vais pas toujours...). Multi-word adverbial phrases (une fois par semaine, etc.) can go at the start or end of the sentence.

topics.title: Prendre (to take) and Sortir (to go out)

items.fr: je prends / tu prends / il prend
nous prenons / vous prenez / ils prennent
je sors / tu sors / il sort
nous sortons / vous sortez / ils sortent

topics.rule: Sortir-type verbs (dormir, s'endormir, partir, servir) have two stems: singular forms drop the last 3 letters of the infinitive, plural forms drop only the last 2.

items.fr: je me promène sur la plage
items.en: I go for a walk on the beach

topics.title: The comparative

items.fr: Jacques est plus grand que Julie.

items.en: better (irregular comparative of bon — 'plus bon' doesn't exist)

topics.rule: que becomes qu' before a vowel. The adjective agrees with the sentence's subject, not the comparison target.

topics.title: The superlative

items.fr: Le sport le plus intéressant, c'est le rugby.
items.en: The most interesting sport is rugby.
best / worst (irregular, come before the noun like BAGS adjectives)

topics.rule: Superlative uses definite article + plus/moins + adjective; 'de' after the superlative translates 'in' (la plus grande ville du monde). meilleur/pire and BAGS-type adjectives (beau, nouveau, vieux, bon, gentil, mauvais, grand, petit, gros, haut, large, bref) go BEFORE the noun even in the superlative.

topics.title: Dates and birthdays

items.fr: Quelle est la date de ton anniversaire?

topics.rule: French uses cardinal numbers for dates (le 3 octobre), not ordinal numbers like English's 'the third'.

topics.title: Asking questions: est-ce que and inversion

items.en: Where do you live? (est-ce que form)

items.fr: où / quand / comment / pourquoi / qui / combien / quel(le)
items.en: where / when / how / why / who / how much-many / which-what

topics.rule: Two main ways to form a question: (1) question word + est-ce que + normal word order, or (2) inversion of the verb and subject pronoun (more formal/written).

topics.title: Colours
topics.rule: Colours come after the noun and agree in number/gender. Colours already ending in -e (rose, orange, rouge) don't double the e in feminine; those ending in -s (gris) don't double s in masc. plural. Orange and marron are invariable (never agree). Add 'clair' (light) or 'foncé' (dark) after a colour and it becomes invariable too (bleu foncé).

items.fr: je mets / tu mets / il met
nous mettons / vous mettez / ils mettent

topics.title: Interrogative adjectives (quel)
topics.rule: Quel(le)(s) agrees with the noun that follows it, or with the noun referred to by est/sont (Quelle est ta cravate préférée?).

topics.title: Demonstrative adjectives (ce, cet, cette, ces)
topics.rule: Ce (masc.), cet (masc. before vowel/silent h), cette (fem.), ces (plural). Add -ci/-là to the noun to distinguish 'this/these' from 'that/those'.

items.en: What material is/are your... made of?

topics.title: Demonstrative pronouns (celui, ceux, celle, celles)
topics.rule: Demonstrative pronouns agree in gender/number with the noun they replace, and are often followed by 'de' (celui de Gérard), 'qui' (ceux qui sont en noir), or -ci/-là.

items.fr: Tu aimes...? / Est-ce que tu aimes...?
... il/elle te plaît? / ils/elles te plaisent?
items.en: do you like it/them? (lit. does it/do they please you)

items.fr: un sac à main / un sac à dos

topics.title: Vouloir and Pouvoir

items.fr: je veux / tu veux / il veut
nous voulons / vous voulez / ils veulent
je peux / tu peux / il peut
nous pouvons / vous pouvez / ils peuvent

topics.rule: Both take an infinitive directly after them (je veux sortir). In the negative, ne...pas wraps the conjugated verb only: Je ne veux pas sortir.

topics.title: Direct object pronouns
topics.rule: Unlike English, French direct object pronouns go BEFORE the verb (Je le prends = I take it). ne...pas wraps both the pronoun and the verb (Nicolas ne m'appelle pas).

topics.title: The partitive (du, de la, de l', des)
topics.rule: The partitive translates 'some' or unspecified quantity, used mainly with uncountable/abstract nouns. It becomes just 'de' after ne...pas (except with être), after quantity expressions (une bouteille de), and before an adjective+plural noun (de bonnes notes). Verbs like adorer/aimer/préférer/détester take the definite article instead (j'aime le café, not du café).

items.fr: un poisson / du thon / du saumon
un dessert / du gâteau / de la glace
Qu'est-ce que vous prenez au petit-déjeuner?
items.en: What do you have for breakfast?

items.fr: le marchand de fruits et légumes

topics.title: The pronoun 'y' (there)

items.fr: Tu vas à la boulangerie? Non, j'y vais demain.
items.en: Are you going to the bakery? No, I'm going (there) tomorrow.

topics.rule: 'Y' replaces à + [place] and goes before the verb. Unlike English (where 'there' can be dropped), 'y' must be included in French.

items.fr: je mange / tu manges / il mange
nous mangeons / vous mangez / ils mangent
je bois / tu bois / il boit
nous buvons / vous buvez / ils boivent

topics.title: The futur proche (aller + infinitive)
topics.rule: aller (conjugated) + infinitive describes near-future, inevitable, or pre-planned events. Only the first verb (aller) is conjugated.

topics.title: Expressions of quantity + de

items.fr: un kilo de / un demi-kilo de
items.en: a kilo of / half a kilo of

items.fr: un litre de / un demi-litre de
items.en: a litre of / half a litre of

items.fr: une tasse de / un verre de / un bol de
items.en: a cup of / a glass of / a bowl of

topics.rule: After quantity expressions ending in 'de', use just 'de' — never the full partitive (du/de la/des).

topics.title: The pronoun 'en'

items.fr: Tu veux du café? Oui, j'en veux.
items.en: Do you want coffee? Yes, I want some (of it).
No, I don't have any (of them).

topics.rule: 'En' replaces a partitive or quantity expression + noun, and goes before the verb. It has no direct English equivalent (often 'of it/them', frequently dropped in English).

items.en: Can you give me the menu?

items.fr: Quel est le plat du jour?
Je voudrais un steak saignant/à point/bien cuit.

topics.title: The passé composé — regular verbs with avoir
topics.rule: Regular passé composé = present tense of avoir + past participle. -er verbs: -é; -ir verbs: -i; -re verbs: -u. Used for completed past actions or a change of state.

topics.title: The passé composé — adverbs as time markers
topics.rule: Short common adverbs (déjà, bien, souvent, trop, vraiment...) go between avoir and the past participle. Longer adverbs of manner tend to follow the past participle. Time expressions often go at the start or end of the sentence.

topics.title: The passé composé — irregular past participles
topics.rule: These past participles are irregular and must be memorised individually; they still combine with a conjugated avoir.

topics.title: Savoir vs Connaître

items.fr: je sais / tu sais / il sait
items.en: I/you/he know(s) (a fact, how to do something)

items.fr: nous savons / vous savez / ils savent
je connais / tu connais / il connaît
items.en: I/you/he know(s) / am/is familiar with (a person, place, work)

items.fr: nous connaissons / vous connaissez / ils connaissent

topics.rule: Savoir = knowledge of facts, or 'know how to' + infinitive. Connaître = familiarity with people, places, or creative works.

topics.title: The passé composé — être-governed verbs

items.en: to go up / to go down
to be born / to die (irregular participles: né, mort)
to come back / to become (modelled on venir)

topics.rule: Around 14 verbs of movement/state (mnemonic: MRS VAN DER TRAMP) take être instead of avoir in the passé composé, and the past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject (elle est allée, ils sont partis).

topics.title: Reflexive verbs in the passé composé
topics.rule: Reflexive verbs always take être in the passé composé, with the past participle agreeing with the subject — UNLESS a direct object noun follows the verb (elle s'est lavé les mains — no agreement, because 'les mains' is the direct object, not the reflexive pronoun).

topics.title: Disjunctive (emphatic) pronouns
topics.rule: Used to emphasise a subject (Moi, je parle français), before/after et or ou joining people, in short answers with no verb (Qui parle français? — Moi!), after c'est/ce n'est pas, and after most prepositions (avec elle, pour lui).

items.en: I know how to do DIY.
I know how to work in a team.
